content: Ectoderm-neural cortex protein 1 (ENC1) is a protein encoded by the ENC1 gene in humans. Function: The wild-type p53 tumor suppressor protein (TP53) is activated in response to DNA damage or hyperproliferative signals. This activation leads to either cell cycle arrest or apoptosis. Mutations that inactivate p53 are found in approximately 50% of all tumors. In a study conducted by Polyak et al. (1997), serial analysis of gene expression (SAGE) was used to assess mRNA levels in a colorectal cancer cell line that had been transfected with p53. Out of 7,202 transcripts identified, only 14 were expressed at levels more than 10 times higher in cells expressing p53 compared to control cells. These genes were termed p53-induced genes (PIGs) by the researchers. Several of these genes were predicted to encode proteins involved in redox regulation. The study highlighted that reactive oxygen species (ROS) are strong inducers of apoptosis. Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated that p53 expression leads to ROS production, which increases as apoptosis progresses under certain conditions. Among the PIGs, the PIG10 gene, also known as ENC1, was found to encode an actin-binding protein. Interactions: ENC1 has been shown to interact with the Retinoblastoma protein. Model Organisms: Model organisms have been utilized to study the function of ENC1. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Enc1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was developed at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute. Both male and female mice underwent a standardized phenotypic screening process to evaluate the effects of ENC1 deletion. Additional specialized screens, including in-depth immunological phenotyping, were also conducted.
